title_en: This Is How New York City Takes Out Its Trash
title_zh: 纽约市如何收垃圾：专访清洁局（DSNY）副局长 Joshua Goodman
subtitle_zh: 从黑垃圾袋到街边集装箱化，纽约“垃圾革命”如何用数据重塑850万人的倒垃圾方式
description: This Is How New York City Takes Out Its Trash

turns.en: Bloomberg Audio Studios.
turns.zh: Bloomberg Audio Studios。

turns.en: Podcasts. Radio. News.
turns.zh: 播客。广播。新闻。

turns.en: Hello and welcome to another episode of the Odd Thoughts Podcast.
turns.zh: 大家好，欢迎收听新一期的 Odd Lots 播客。

turns.en: I'm Tracy Alloway.
turns.zh: 我是 Tracy Alloway。

turns.en: And I'm Joe Weisenthal.
turns.zh: 我是 Joe Weisenthal。

turns.en: Joe, I was talking trash with a guy at a party recently.
turns.zh: Joe，我前阵子在一个派对上跟人聊起了垃圾。

turns.en: Go on.
turns.zh: 继续说。

turns.en: No, I met this guy at a party.
turns.zh: 不是，我在派对上认识了这么一个人。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.en: And you know some people... Are so into their work.
turns.zh: 你知道的，有些人……特别投入自己的工作。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: An area of expertise that they just start talking to you about it. And this guy happened to be an expert in trash.
turns.zh: 有个自己特别擅长的领域，一开口就跟你聊个不停。而这个人恰好是垃圾方面的专家。

turns.en: That's really cool. I don't know much about trash.
turns.zh: 那真挺酷的。我对垃圾了解不多。

turns.en: I'm impressed at like what a complex logistical operation it must be to collect trash in a city like New York City.
turns.zh: 我很惊叹，在纽约这样一座城市里收垃圾，得是多么复杂的一项后勤运作。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: I also understand that, you know, it's sort of one of those classic things where, isn't there a cliche like, There's no Democrat or Republican way to pick up trash. Some famous politician once said that, and they were talking about city management and what makes city management different than other sort of political things. It's like the trash isn't picked up, it's not picked up, and it's not an ideological thing.
turns.zh: 我也知道，这算是那种经典说法之一——不是有句老话嘛，收垃圾没有民主党或共和党之分。某位名人说过这话，他讲的是城市管理，以及城市管理和其他政治事务有什么不同。就是说，垃圾要是没被收走，那就是没被收走，这不是意识形态的事。

turns.en: Well, it's interesting you say that because the person I was talking to at this party who we're about to have on the show as a guest described Trash Collection in New York City as one of the last services untouched by neoliberalism. And that's when I knew we had to have him on Oddlots. And then he introduced his wife as his garbage queen. And then I was doubly sure that we needed to have.
turns.zh: 有意思的是你这么说，因为我在派对上聊的那个人——也就是我们马上要请来上节目的嘉宾——把纽约市的垃圾收运描述为最后一项未被新自由主义（neoliberalism）触及的公共服务。就在那一刻我知道我们必须请他上 Odd Lots。然后他还介绍他太太说她是他的“垃圾女王”。于是我更加确定我们得请……

turns.en: Him on Oddlots. But Trash Collection is such a fascinating thing. I wasn't planning.
turns.zh: ……他上 Odd Lots。不过垃圾收运真是件特别迷人的事。我本来没打算……

turns.en: on doing an episode on it, but I've been converted, I guess, after this conversation, because you think about in a city like New York, just how much trash has to be dealt with on a daily basis. And obviously in New York specifically, it's not like we're putting it, you know, in the city.
turns.zh: ……做一期关于它的节目，但我想我在这场对话之后被说服了。因为你想想在纽约这样的城市，每天要处理掉多少垃圾。而且显然在纽约这里，我们并不是把垃圾就堆在城里。

turns.en: We have to find other places to store our trash.
turns.zh: 我们得找别的地方来存放我们的垃圾。

turns.en: And at the same time, New York City is not well known for being the cleanest place in the world. In fact, we famously stick our garbage out in bags on the curb.
turns.zh: 与此同时，纽约市也并不以全世界最干净的地方著称。事实上，我们出了名地把垃圾装在袋子里扔到路边。

turns.en: And wait for collection.
turns.zh: 然后等着被收走。

turns.en: And we are in a giant process of trying to change that. So there's a lot to discuss here.
turns.zh: 而且我们正在经历一场试图改变这一现状的巨大工程。所以这里有很多可聊的。

turns.en: There's a lot to discuss.
turns.zh: 确实有很多可聊的。

turns.en: By the way, that quote, according to Google Gemini, there's no Republican or Democratic way to pick up the garbage. Former Mayor Fiorello LaGuardia was the one who said that. And so Who is out running as a Republican on a fusion nonpartisan?
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，那句话，根据 Google Gemini 的说法，“收垃圾没有共和党或民主党之分”，是前市长 Fiorello LaGuardia 说的。所以现在有一位以共和党身份、走融合票（fusion）、无党派路线出来竞选的人……

turns.en: Anyway, that's not the point. But it is, you know, it's just a thing. Either you do it well or you don't.
turns.zh: 总之，这不是重点。但这确实是，你知道的，就是这么回事：要么你把它做好，要么就没做好。

turns.en: And people get really upset if you don't. New York is tricky for multiple reasons. But, you know, you think in a suburb, right, you put the trash out. But there aren't cars in the way between the trash bins and the garbage truck, etc. Because they're in the driveway or the garage or something like that.
turns.zh: 如果你没做好，大家会非常不满。纽约因为多种原因而棘手。但你想想在郊区，对吧，你把垃圾放出去，但垃圾桶和垃圾车之间不会有车挡着等等，因为车都停在车道或车库里之类的。

turns.en: New York has all kinds of things in between the road and the bins. I know there's, you know, there's.
turns.zh: 纽约在马路和垃圾桶之间有各种各样的障碍物。我知道有，你懂的，有……

turns.en: This big effort to do containerization, I think, at one point or headlines about some, you know, outside study from like McKinsey, etc. There's a lot of interesting logistical questions about trash collection. And so it's a core topic. Even though we haven't done it, it sits firmly.
turns.zh: 有一项推行集装箱化（containerization）的大工程，我记得某个时候有过头条，说什么外部研究，比如 McKinsey 做的等等。关于垃圾收运有很多有意思的后勤问题。所以这是个核心话题。尽管我们还没做过，它稳稳地落在……

turns.en: In our wheelhouse.
turns.zh: ……我们的专长范围里。

turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.en: All right.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.en: So without further ado, we have the perfect guest. We're going to be speaking with Joshua Goodman. He is, of course, Deputy Commissioner at New York City's Department of Sanitation. So Josh, thanks so much for.
turns.zh: 那么话不多说，我们请到了完美的嘉宾。我们要对话的是 Joshua Goodman。他当然是纽约市清洁局（Department of Sanitation）的副局长。Josh，非常感谢你……

turns.en: Coming on All Lots.
turns.zh: ……来做客 Odd Lots。

turns.en: Thank you both for having me.
turns.zh: 谢谢你们两位邀请我。

turns.en: Is trash collection apolitical?
turns.zh: 垃圾收运是与政治无关的吗？

turns.en: So obviously we all admire and respect Mayor LaGuardia. It's a famous quote.
turns.zh: 显然我们都敬佩和尊重 LaGuardia 市长。这是句名言。

turns.en: You hear it all the time. You hear paraphrases of it all the time. It's patently untrue, right?
turns.zh: 你老是听到它，老是听到各种转述。但它明显是不成立的，对吧？

turns.en: The moment you start to dissect it, you realize that, of course, an enormous public space logistical initiative is going to be colored by ideology. Partisanship, maybe not, but the sort of implication behind the quote that it's a binary, yes, it's picked up, no, it's not picked up, really undersells substantially the amount of planning that needs to go into this, both in the short term and in the long term. In New York City, we at the Department of Sanitation pick up, process, and export 24 million pounds of trash recycling and compostable material every single day. One of the things I like to tell people is that there's a word that you'll hear a lot, Sisyphean, right?
turns.zh: 一旦你开始拆解它，你就会意识到，当然，一项庞大的公共空间后勤工程必然会被意识形态所染。党派之争也许不至于，但这句名言背后暗含的那种“非黑即白——要么收走了，要么没收走”的二元论，其实大大低估了这件事所需的规划量，无论是短期还是长期。在纽约市，我们清洁局每天要收运、处理并输出 2400 万磅的垃圾、回收物和可堆肥物料。我喜欢跟人们讲的一点是，有个词你会经常听到——西西弗斯式的（Sisyphean），对吧？

turns.en: And you hear it used imprecisely, in my opinion.
turns.zh: 而我觉得你会听到它被用得不精确。

turns.en: It's often used as just a synonym for hard. Oh, I, you know, school was a Sisyphean task or this home improvement project, whatever.
turns.zh: 它常常被当成“难”的同义词。哦，我，你知道的，上学是件西西弗斯式的苦差事，或者这个家装项目，诸如此类。

turns.en: But it ended.
turns.zh: 但它总归会结束。

turns.en: Right. And we have the definitional Sisyphean task. Just as Sisyphus faced the boulder again each day, we pick up 24 million pounds today. We pick up 24 million pounds tomorrow. We pick up 24 million pounds the next day. There will never be a time when DSNY says, great news, everyone.
turns.zh: 对。而我们手上有的是定义级别的西西弗斯式任务。就像西西弗斯每天都重新面对那块巨石，我们今天收 2400 万磅，明天收 2400 万磅，后天再收 2400 万磅。永远不会有一天 DSNY 会宣布：“好消息，各位——”

turns.en: We got it all. Exactly.
turns.zh: “——我们全收完了。”正是如此。

turns.en: And this is, as Tracy mentioned, we think of it as the last free unlimited service.
turns.zh: 而且这就像 Tracy 提到的，我们把它看作最后一项免费的、无限量服务。

turns.en: There's no signup. There's no opt-in.
turns.zh: 不用注册。不用 opt-in。

turns.en: There's no means test. You put it out, we come and get it. It's basically us in the public library at this point. And that means, and that's specific to New York, of course, but it means that as we think about changes in global best practices, We need to keep that commitment to full universal service.
turns.zh: 没有经济状况调查（means test）。你把它放出来，我们就来收。基本上现在就剩我们和公共图书馆还是这样了。而这——当然这是纽约特有的——意味着当我们思考全球最佳实践的变化时，我们需要坚守对全民普遍服务的那份承诺。

turns.en: I don't want to.
turns.zh: 我不想……

turns.en: Get too bogged down in this question of Sisyphean and the philosophy of what the Greeks were trying to teach with the lesson of Sisyphus and the philosophers like Camus and so forth who studied Sisyphus.
turns.zh: ……太陷入这个西西弗斯式的问题，也不想陷进希腊人想借西西弗斯的教训教给我们什么、以及像 Camus 这些研究过西西弗斯的哲学家……

turns.en: Over the years.
turns.zh: ……这些年来……

turns.en: But one element of that lesson is the boulder, yes, it was endless and it never ended, much like trash collection. but there was no purpose to it. There was no internal satisfaction that one could perceive from the outside, whereas helping the public, that could in theory be satisfactory. So had Sisyphus pushed up the boulder every day and then something great happened to the land, oh, it was clean, maybe that would have been satisfying internally. And what's tortuous about the Sisyphean metaphor is that there does not seem to be any reward for it.
turns.zh: ……但那教训里有一个元素是：那块巨石，是的，它永无止境、永远没有尽头，很像垃圾收运；但它没有任何目的。从外部无法感知到任何内在的满足感，而帮助公众，理论上倒是能带来满足。所以假如西西弗斯每天把巨石推上去，然后这片土地上发生了很棒的事——哦，它变干净了——也许那会带来内在的满足。而西西弗斯式比喻之所以折磨人，就在于它似乎没有任何回报。

turns.en: Well, it is true that most New Yorkers think of cleanliness as the natural state, right? It's not, wow, you did a great job.
turns.zh: 嗯，确实，大多数纽约人把干净视为一种自然状态，对吧？不是“哇，你干得真棒”。

turns.en: Are you sure about that?
turns.zh: 你确定是这样吗？

turns.en: Well, that's the goal, right?
turns.zh: 嗯，那是目标，对吧？

turns.en: The idea is that a street is supposed to be clean.
turns.zh: 这个理念是：一条街道本就应该干净。

turns.en: And you mentioned Camus.
turns.zh: 你还提到了 Camus。

turns.en: Our guy at sanitation has actually started because many people notice black bags of trash. They notice piles of trash. They rarely, if ever, notice the absence of piles of trash. And so there is a philosophical element to this, but obviously- I know we're going to spend a lot more time on.
turns.zh: 我们清洁局有个人真的开始……因为很多人会注意到成堆的黑垃圾袋。他们会注意到一堆堆的垃圾。他们却很少、甚至从来不会注意到“没有垃圾堆”这件事。所以这里面是有哲学成分的，但显然——我知道我们今天会花更多时间讲……

turns.en: The details today.
turns.zh: ……细节。

turns.en: We could just talk about Camus and Sartre.
turns.zh: 我们完全可以就聊 Camus 和 Sartre。

turns.en: The whole time.
turns.zh: 聊一整期。

turns.en: What it really came down to was about four or five years ago, we had spent decades of people coming to New York from Barcelona, from Buenos Aires, from Paris, from London, even from Chicago and LA and saying, why do you live like this? And for many decades, our answer had basically been like, well, have you tried a bagel? We have better pizza than you do. We had not gotten serious about addressing these challenges in a meaningful, long-term way. And that's what's begun to change over the last few years through a process that we call the trash revolution, which is a complete reimagining of the relationship that 8.5 million New Yorkers have with 24 million pounds of trash a day, what they expect from us, what we expect from them. And it's required an enormous amount of data analysis, of streetscape redesign, of work across agencies, of breaking down silos. And fortunately, it's getting results. There's a lot we can talk about that really shows that this is working.
turns.zh: 真正归结起来是，大约四五年前，我们花了几十年时间，人们从 Barcelona、从 Buenos Aires、从 Paris、从 London，甚至从 Chicago 和 LA 来到纽约，说：“你们怎么能这样生活？”而几十年来，我们的回答基本上就是：“那你尝过贝果（bagel）吗？我们的披萨比你们的好吃。”我们一直没有认真地去以有意义的、长期的方式应对这些挑战。而这正是过去几年开始改变的东西，通过一个我们称之为“垃圾革命”（trash revolution）的进程——那是对 850 万纽约人与每天 2400 万磅垃圾之间关系的一次彻底重塑：他们对我们有什么期待，我们对他们有什么期待。它需要大量的数据分析、街景重新设计、跨部门协作、打破部门壁垒。所幸，它正在见效。有很多东西可讲，能真正说明这套做法在起作用。

turns.en: Before we get into all the ins and outs of the trash revolution, which I love as a designation, how did black bags of garbage become a thing in New York in the first place? Because I remember this was one of the big culture shocks when I first moved to New York. college and then I dropped out. So I was only here for two or three weeks. Maybe all the trash bags had something to do with it. But walking down the street, coming from places like London and Tokyo and seeing these bags of trash laid out, it was kind of weird. Yeah.
turns.zh: 在我们深入“垃圾革命”的方方面面之前——我很喜欢这个说法——黑色垃圾袋最初是怎么在纽约成为常态的？因为我还记得这是我刚搬到纽约时最大的文化冲击之一。我上大学，然后退学了，所以我在这儿只待了两三周。也许满街的垃圾袋跟这事也有点关系。但走在街上，从 London、Tokyo 这样的地方来，看到这些垃圾袋摊在那儿，感觉挺怪的。是啊。

turns.en: There were really two key events that led to New York's unique status here. One is the 1811 street grid. In New York City, the only non-renewable resource is public space. There is a finite amount of room. And so when the streets were laid out in the 1811 master plan, The city was built without alleyways. You go to Chicago, which has similar density, there are alleys behind almost all buildings to store the trash. So if you're watching a movie and it's set in New York and someone jumps out of a dark alley, it's almost certainly shot in Chicago or an LA soundstage because we don't.
turns.zh: 真正有两个关键事件造就了纽约在这里的独特处境。其一是 1811 年的街道网格规划。在纽约市，唯一不可再生的资源就是公共空间。空间是有限的。所以当 1811 年总体规划铺设街道时，这座城市在建设时没有留后巷（alleyways）。你去 Chicago，它的密度类似，那里几乎所有建筑后面都有巷子来存放垃圾。所以如果你看电影，故事设定在纽约，有人从一条黑巷里跳出来，那几乎可以肯定是在 Chicago 或 LA 的摄影棚拍的，因为我们这儿其实……

turns.en: Really have them.
turns.zh: ……没有巷子。

turns.en: So that meant there was no storage space behind the buildings, which other cities have.
turns.zh: 所以那就意味着建筑后面没有存储空间，而其他城市是有的。

turns.en: And then throughout.
turns.zh: 然后在整个……

turns.en: Much of the 19th and 20th century, the city used sort of the old Oscar the Grouch metal garbage cans. Following the 1968 sanitation strike, the last major New York City sanitation labor action, there was an overflowing amount more than those metal cans can handle. And when the strike was resolved, Mayor Lindsay put together a group to study a number of after effects of the issues the city had faced during that time, one of which was a task force called the Committee on the Black Bag. It studied plastic trash bags, which were basically new at that time, and the plastics industry pushed them as rodent resistant, which obviously we know they're not. And you can easily find New York Times coverage from that time of people proudly stating that the transition from metal garbage cans to black bags will reduce rats while freeing up public space. Obviously, it became clear almost immediately that that was not the case, but it took another five decades or so to get serious about promoting a new solution.
turns.zh: ……19 和 20 世纪的大部分时间里，这座城市用的是那种老式的、Oscar the Grouch 式的金属垃圾桶。在 1968 年清洁工人大罢工——纽约市最后一次重大清洁劳工行动——之后，垃圾量溢出了那些金属桶所能承受的程度。罢工解决后，Lindsay 市长组建了一个小组来研究那段时间城市所面临问题的诸多后续影响，其中一个特别工作组叫做“黑袋委员会”（Committee on the Black Bag）。它研究了塑料垃圾袋——当时基本还是新东西——塑料行业把它们推销为“防鼠”，而我们现在当然知道它们并不防鼠。你很容易就能找到当时《New York Times》的报道，人们自豪地宣称，从金属垃圾桶过渡到黑袋子会减少老鼠，同时腾出公共空间。显然，几乎立刻就证明并非如此，但又过了大约五十年，人们才开始认真推动一个新的解决方案。

turns.en: So I understand, and we're going to get into this, that there are different approaches, etc., to picking up the trash, etc., But why is the LaGuardia quote wrong? I understand different views, but that still doesn't necessarily mean, to me, it still seems like it could be right in the sense that different views don't necessarily map to politics.
turns.zh: 所以据我理解——我们后面会深入——收垃圾有不同的方法等等。但为什么 LaGuardia 那句话是错的？我理解有不同观点，但那在我看来仍然不一定意味着……它仍可能是对的，因为不同观点不一定就对应到政治。

turns.en: It is true that it's not a neat left-right split necessarily, but it's not true that who you put into office has no bearing on what happens to the trash. I think his point was that it transcends ideology, and it doesn't, or else this would have been done a long time ago.
turns.zh: 确实，它不一定是一个清晰的左右之分，但“你把谁选上台对垃圾的处境毫无影响”这一点并不成立。我想他的意思是它超越了意识形态，但它并没有，否则这事早就做成了。

turns.en: Okay, then what are the different ideological frameworks from which we can view the question of optimal trash collection?
turns.zh: 好，那么我们可以从哪些不同的意识形态框架来看待“最优垃圾收运”这个问题？

turns.en: One of the things to think about is that cleanliness is not just a an abstract concept. It has a tremendous impact on a person's quality of life. Every morning, hundreds of thousands of New Yorkers get up, they go out, they go to work, they go to school. If they walk down a dirty street, the first thing they think is no one cares about me. And I can't necessarily blame people for feeling that way. Often, thoughts about cleanliness in public space are....
turns.zh: 要考虑的一点是，清洁不只是一个抽象概念。它对一个人的生活质量有巨大影响。每天早上，成千上万的纽约人起床、出门、上班、上学。如果他们走在一条脏兮兮的街上，他们脑海里冒出的第一件事就是：“没人在乎我。”我不一定能怪人们有这种感觉。通常，关于公共空间清洁的思考……

turns.en: You have to think about who you're prioritizing, right?
turns.zh: ……你得想清楚你在优先照顾谁，对吧？

turns.en: So Is it someone who spends the bulk of their time in public in a car versus someone who spends the bulk of their time in public walking? Is it someone for whom a rat is a curiosity versus a reality that they have to live with?
turns.zh: 那么，是那个大部分公共时间都待在车里的人，还是那个大部分公共时间都在步行的人？是那个把老鼠当成一件稀奇事的人，还是那个不得不与老鼠共存、把老鼠当作现实的人？

turns.en: I kind of like the rats.
turns.zh: 我倒是有点喜欢老鼠。

turns.en: I get really bored walking down the street and seeing some wildlife, which in New York City is just pigeons and rats.
turns.zh: 我走在街上特别无聊的时候，看到点野生动物还挺有意思——而在纽约市，野生动物就是鸽子和老鼠。

turns.en: It's somewhat entertaining.
turns.zh: 这多少算是种消遣。

turns.en: I get it. Look, I love all animals. I'm a longtime vegan.
turns.zh: 我懂。瞧，我爱所有动物。我是长期的纯素食者（vegan）。

turns.en: But the fact is that There is a Jungian reaction to a rat for most people. You walk down a street in New York and a rat runs across your foot. You remember it every time you're on the block for the rest of your life. And the same goes for public space trash, which I know certain New Yorkers have sort of romanticized.
turns.zh: 但事实是，对大多数人来说，看到老鼠会有一种荣格式（Jungian）的反应。你走在纽约的街上，一只老鼠从你脚上跑过，你这辈子每次走到那个街区都会记得。公共空间的垃圾也一样，我知道某些纽约人有点把它浪漫化了。

turns.en: I think that you can.
turns.zh: 我觉得你是可以……

turns.en: Only do that if it's not your reality. You know, that living around trash and rats is not a good thing. And we would like it to, you know. People sometimes assume that anyone at the Department of Sanitation loves the trash. And I always tell them, no, no, no, our job is to get rid of it.
turns.zh: ……只有当那不是你的现实时才能那样浪漫化。你知道的，生活在垃圾和老鼠周围并不是好事。我们希望它……人们有时以为清洁局任何人都热爱垃圾。我总是跟他们说：不不不，我们的工作是把它清除掉。

turns.en: We hate the trash.
turns.zh: 我们讨厌垃圾。

turns.en: The trash is our enemy, as fascinating as it is to study. And so when we thought about putting.
turns.zh: 垃圾是我们的敌人，尽管研究起来很迷人。所以当我们考虑把……

turns.en: Global best practices into place just the last.
turns.zh: ……全球最佳实践落地的时候，就在最近这……

turns.en: Few years, this is actually a very data-driven agency, probably not surprising. But we had about a century of data about the weight of the trash, which had long been our primary metric for efficiencies. And what we needed was data about the volume of the trash. That's what you need for containerization programs. And so we had to do a 70,000 block volumetric analysis. We went block by block and converted those weights into volumes and developed the programs that are coming out now. And there were a lot of different, both left and right, thoughts about what approach we should take, if any.
turns.zh: ……几年，这其实是一个非常数据驱动的部门，大概不意外。但我们有大约一个世纪的垃圾重量数据，重量长期以来是我们衡量效率的主要指标。而我们真正需要的是垃圾体积（volume）的数据。那才是集装箱化项目所需要的。所以我们不得不做一次覆盖 70,000 个街区的体积分析。我们逐个街区地把那些重量换算成体积，并开发出现在正在推出的这些项目。关于该采取哪种方法（如果有的话），左派右派都有很多不同的想法。

turns.en: And.

We've developed a strategy that we think will work for the unique streetscape of New York. When I first got involved in this work, I would often hear from people, well, there's no place as dense as New York that does this.
turns.zh: ……我们制定了一套我们认为适合纽约独特街景的战略。当我刚开始参与这项工作时，我常常听到人们说：“没有哪个像纽约这么密的地方这么做的。”

turns.en: Not true.
turns.zh: 不是真的。

turns.en: There's no place with as much weather flexibility as New York.
turns.zh: “没有哪个地方像纽约这样有如此大的天气弹性。”

turns.en: Not true. There's no place that produces as much volume of trash. Not true.
turns.zh: 不是真的。“没有哪个地方产生像纽约这么大的垃圾量。”不是真的。

turns.en: We actually produce per person less trash than most other Western cities. There's no reason that they can have this everywhere else in the world other than a political inertia, right? And that's what's begun to change based on the data that we've produced.
turns.zh: 实际上我们人均产生的垃圾比大多数其他西方城市要少。除了政治惰性之外，没有任何理由让这套做法在世界其他所有地方都能推行、偏偏在这儿不行，对吧？而这正是基于我们所产出的数据开始改变的东西。

turns.en: Well, to me, one of the obvious political choices that's been made in New York is also.
turns.zh: 嗯，对我来说，纽约做出的一个明显的政治选择还在于……

turns.en: We don't have a pay-as-you-go service, or you're not paying per pound of trash that you produce, right? I can produce a lot of trash, and it's sort of incumbent on the city to collect it versus someone who's trying their best to recycle and compost and things like that. Why don't we talk about logistics for a second just to better understand the current state so that we can figure out where we're trying to get to. I take out a bag of trash from my apartment building and it's a Wednesday in Soho and I place it on the curb. What happens to it from there?
turns.zh: ……我们没有“按量付费”（pay-as-you-go）的服务，你不是按你产生多少磅垃圾来付费，对吧？我可以产生很多垃圾，而收走它在某种程度上是城市的义务；相比之下有人却竭尽所能去回收、堆肥等等。我们为什么不一分钟聊聊后勤，好更好地理解现状，从而弄清楚我们想去哪儿。我从我的公寓楼里拎出一袋垃圾，那是 Soho 的一个星期三，我把它放在路边。从那儿开始它会经历什么？

turns.en: So a collection truck, we don't call them garbage trucks because they also pick up recycling and compost, comes by sometime generally between midnight and 8.30 in the morning. Try to get as much of it done before peak rush hour. The trucks are on routes that are optimized for a few things. They hold about 12 to 13 tons of trash each. You want it to get full on its route, and you want the route to be completed in a single shift. So they're optimized around those factors. And then once the truck is full, or loaded out is the jargon, it's taken to a network of transfer stations.
turns.zh: 那么一辆收运车——我们不叫它们垃圾车，因为它们也收回收物和堆肥物——通常会在午夜到早上 8:30 之间的某个时候过来。尽量在早高峰之前把它做完。这些车跑的路线是针对几件事优化过的。每辆车大约能装 12 到 13 吨垃圾。你希望它在路线上装满，也希望这条路线能在一个班次内跑完。所以是围绕这些因素优化的。然后一旦车装满了——行话叫“loaded out”——它就被送到一个转运站（transfer station）网络。

turns.en: So prior to 2000, it was.
turns.zh: 在 2000 年以前，那是……

turns.en: All taken to the Staten Island landfill. When the landfill closed, the city moved to a waste export model. It was a multi-billion dollar, 15-year infrastructure project to build five transfer stations around the city. These are places where the truck comes, it dumps out onto the tipping floor, a big floor, where a large front-end loader pushes it down holes in the floor into like a shipping container that's underneath. Robotic arms seal up the shipping container. A giant crane puts it on either a barge or a rail car. and it's taken to its final destination outside the city. This is obviously far more environmentally sustainable than an in-city landfill, and also than the old trucking model, right? Barges and rail cars, much, much better for the environment. When you see these barges with 50 or 75 packed storage containers on them, you think, wow, that would have been 75 trucks driving to a landfill.
turns.zh: ……全部送到 Staten Island 的垃圾填埋场。当填埋场关闭后，城市转向了废物外运（waste export）模式。那是一个数十亿美元、为期 15 年的基础设施项目，在全城各处建了五个转运站。在这些地方，卡车过来，把垃圾卸到“倾倒地板”（tipping floor）上——那是一大片地面——一台大型前端装载机把它推进地板上的洞里，落到下面一个类似集装箱的容器里。机械臂把集装箱封好。一台巨型起重机把它放到一艘驳船或一节轨道车上，然后被送到市外的最终目的地。这显然比市内填埋场环保得多，也比旧的卡车运输模式环保得多，对吧？驳船和轨道车，对环境好得多。当你看到这些驳船上装着 50 或 75 个塞满的存储集装箱时，你会想：哇，那本来得是 75 辆卡车开去填埋场。

turns.en: That's for your.
turns.zh: 那是给你的……

turns.en: Regular trash, refuse is the term that appears in our materials. Um, for your metal glass and plastic, they're taken to a facility in sunset park where they're palletized and prepared to be sold on the recycling market. Uh, New York city is a great opportunity for me to mention something really important, which is lots of people in sort of the demographic that listens to odd lots, educated, smart people, the cocktail party set, think that it makes them sound really smart to say, I heard recycling is a scam. Didn't someone once tell me, I have to tell you, I can't speak for other municipalities. New York City's recycling system is protected by long-term contracts that guarantee beneficial reuse of those materials. If you properly sort a can or bottle in New York City, it will become a new can or bottle or other reusable item.
turns.zh: ……普通垃圾——“refuse”（废弃物）是我们材料里用的术语。至于你的金属、玻璃和塑料，它们被送到 Sunset Park 的一处设施，在那里被打托盘、准备好拿到回收市场上出售。纽约市是个很好的机会让我提一件非常重要的事：很多属于听 Odd Lots 那种人群的人——受过教育、聪明的人，鸡尾酒会那拨人——觉得说“我听说回收是个骗局”能让自己听起来很聪明。“不是有人跟我说过嘛……”我得告诉你——我不能替其他城市说话——纽约市的回收系统受长期合同保护，这些合同保证那些物料得到有益的再利用。如果你在纽约市正确地把一个罐子或瓶子分好类，它就会变成一个新的罐子、瓶子或其他可再利用的物品。

turns.en: Wait, slight tangent. What about a styrofoam cup?
turns.zh: 等等，稍微岔一下。那泡沫塑料杯（styrofoam cup）呢？

turns.en: So styrofoams are banned in the city, right? So you shouldn't see them too often. Styrofoam actually hits on the great issue with this. Styrofoam is often used as the archetypical example of a non-recyclable item.
turns.zh: 泡沫塑料在这座城市是被禁的，对吧？所以你不会太常见到。泡沫塑料其实正好点出了这里的重大议题。泡沫塑料常被当作不可回收物品的典型例子。

turns.en: Can't be recycled, can't be recycled.
turns.zh: 不能回收，不能回收。

turns.en: On a pure molecular level, of course it can be recycled.
turns.zh: 从纯粹的分子层面看，它当然可以回收。

turns.en: It's just plastic.
turns.zh: 它不过是塑料。

turns.en: The issue is that it's so light that no plastics manufacturer would ever feel that they had enough in one space to make money off of it. It's a good example of how this is actually a market-based system for recycling specifically, because many more things are recyclable from a chemical standpoint than are actually accepted as recycling. In New York City, you probably know that in 2017, 2018, there were domestic policy changes in China that collapsed a lot of cities.
turns.zh: 问题在于它太轻了，没有哪个塑料制造商会觉得自己在一处攒到了足够多、能靠它赚钱的量。这是个很好的例子，说明回收——尤其是回收——实际上是一套基于市场的系统，因为从化学角度看可回收的东西，远远多于实际被当作回收物来接收的东西。在纽约市，你大概知道，2017、2018 年中国国内的政策变化让很多城市的……

turns.en: Recycling markets.
turns.zh: ……回收市场崩掉了。

turns.en: New York was protected from those changes by long-term strategic planning before that. We also had resisted an urge that a lot of cities gave into in a few years before that to combine their paper and their metal, glass, and plastic.
turns.zh: 纽约靠在那之前的长期战略规划，得以不受那些变化的冲击。我们还抵制住了一种冲动——很多城市在那之前几年屈服于这种冲动——就是把纸类和金属、玻璃、塑料合并在一起。

turns.en: Oh, it's easier for residents.
turns.zh: 哦，那样对居民更方便。

turns.en: It turned out to be a huge money loser for cities that did it and also for the environment when this market change happened in 17, 18.
turns.zh: 结果证明，对那些这么做的城市来说，这是个巨大的亏钱行为；而当 17、18 年这个市场变化发生时，对环境也是如此。

turns.en: What was the argument for doing that?
turns.zh: 当时支持这么做的理由是什么？

turns.en: Because when I think about it in my head, it's like, well, of course it's going to cost more to sort it out.
turns.zh: 因为我脑子里一想，就觉得，嗯，把它分拣出来当然会更费钱。

turns.en: The idea was more people will participate because it's easier, which is a good motivating principle in general. But on this specific topic, the technology is not there yet, or at least we don't feel the technology is there yet. Your paper, just to get back to where it all goes, it goes to Staten Island, where it is actually one of the fastest processes in the waste stream. cardboard and paper that you recycle today might become a new pizza box tomorrow. Pizza boxes are one of the primary things made at that facility. And then your compost, which is sort of our best and newest and most exciting stream. Your food waste goes to a few places, but primarily to our Staten Island compost facility. It's a 33-acre site where over a period of three or four months, we turn and aerate your material until it's broken down into finished compost, which we give away to parks and gardens to residents directly. We just finished our summer compost give back season. We gave away about 15 million pounds of finished compost.
turns.zh: 这个想法是，因为更方便，会有更多人参与——这大体上是个不错的激励原则。但在这个具体议题上，技术还没到位，或者至少我们觉得技术还没到位。说到你的纸类最终去了哪儿——它去 Staten Island，那里其实是废物流中处理最快的环节之一。你今天回收的纸板箱和纸，明天可能就成了一个新的披萨盒。披萨盒是那处设施生产的主要产品之一。然后是你的堆肥，那算是我们最好、最新、最激动人心的一个流。你的厨余垃圾会去到几个地方，但主要去我们 Staten Island 的堆肥设施。那是一片 33 英亩的场地，在三到四个月的时间里，我们翻堆、通风你的物料，直到它分解成成品堆肥，然后我们把成品免费送给公园、花园，也直接送给居民。我们刚结束了夏季的堆肥回馈季。我们免费送出了大约 1500 万磅的成品堆肥。

turns.en: To New Yorkers.
turns.zh: 送给纽约人。

turns.en: I didn't know you could get New York City compost.
turns.zh: 我都不知道原来能弄到纽约市的堆肥。

turns.en: NYC.gov slash get compost. You can find events near you to get 40 pound bags. And some of it goes to the Department of Environmental Protection's Newtown Creek Digestor Eggs. If you've been on the BQE right as you go over the Cushesco and come between Brooklyn and Queens, you'll see the big eggs. Those are large facilities where your food waste will be mixed with wastewater. So it gets mixed there with everything that you put down the sink or that you flush down the toilet where it's digested into biosolids for fertilizer and usable biogas that heats homes in Brooklyn. So your waste goes to a lot of different places, but the idea is to divert as much of it as possible to beneficial use and hopefully to reduce the total amount over time.
turns.zh: NYC.gov 斜杠 get compost。你能找到你附近的活动，去领 40 磅装的袋子。还有一部分会送到环境保护局（Department of Environmental Protection）的 Newtown Creek 消化蛋（Digestor Eggs）。如果你上过 BQE，就在你驶过 Kosciuszko 桥、来到 Brooklyn 和 Queens 之间的时候，你会看到那些大“蛋”。那是些大型设施，你的厨余垃圾会在那里与废水混合。所以它会在那里和你倒进水槽或冲下马桶的所有东西混在一起，被消化成用作肥料的生物固体（biosolids），以及可用的沼气——那些沼气给 Brooklyn 的家庭供暖。所以你的废弃物会去到很多不同的地方，但这个理念是尽可能多地把分流出来做有益利用，并希望能随着时间推移减少总量。

turns.en: I'm thinking about that guy, and it's a guy, at the cocktail party. It's like the classic, like, I heard two-minute segment on.
turns.zh: 我在想鸡尾酒会上那个人——而且是个男的。就是那种经典的，“我听过一段两分钟的……”

turns.en: The radio once.
I hate that guy.
turns.zh: 我真讨厌那种人。

turns.en: I think Outlawed's listeners are better than that. They only say things if they've researched the topic for at least 30 minutes.
turns.zh: 我觉得 Odd Lots 的听众比那种人强。他们只有在把一个话题研究了至少 30 分钟之后才会开口。

turns.en: They certainly... I'm sure Outlawed's listeners know that person, at least.
turns.zh: 他们当然……我确信 Odd Lots 的听众至少认得那种人。

turns.en: They know.
turns.zh: 他们认得。

turns.en: Oh, my God. They're prepared to take it on.
turns.zh: 我的天。他们准备好去迎战了。

turns.en: I can't stand that person. On the other hand, and I don't want to get into this.
turns.zh: 我真受不了那种人。话说回来，而且我不想扯进这个。

turns.en: It might.
turns.zh: 这可能……

turns.en: The fact that, like, New York has guaranteed contracts....
turns.zh: 就是，纽约有保障性的合同这一事实……

turns.en: Anyway.
turns.zh: 总之。

turns.en: Does not necessarily... vindicate recycling. I might vindicate it from the New York City perspective, but let's move on.
turns.zh: 并不一定就……证明了回收是对的。也许从纽约市的角度它能自证，但我们还是往下说吧。

turns.en: All right. That's an rough overview of, let's say, the old regime.
turns.zh: 好。那大致就是，姑且说，旧体制的一个概览。

turns.en: Why don't you give us the equivalent sort of like rough So the big changes in what I just described were that were conducted between 2000 and 2015 to move from a landfill model to a waste export model.
turns.zh: 你为什么不给我们讲讲对应的、粗略的——我刚才描述的那些重大变化，是在 2000 到 2015 年间进行的，从填埋场模式转向废物外运模式。

turns.en: Those were huge back of house changes on our operations. And what we're doing now is making sort of front of house changes for how New Yorkers interact with the trash.
turns.zh: 那些是我们运营上巨大的“后厨”（back of house）层面的变化。而我们现在在做的，是在“前厅”（front of house）层面改变纽约人与垃圾打交道的方式。

turns.en: It's actually, I don't.
turns.zh: 这其实，我不是……

turns.en: Mean to use it as an excuse, but it's one of the reasons why as other cities moved to on-street containerization, New York didn't.
turns.zh: ……想拿它当借口，但这是原因之一：当其他城市转向街边集装箱化（on-street containerization）时，纽约没有。

turns.en: We had this big project going on of building the transfer stations. Obviously, we should be able to do both.
turns.zh: 我们当时正在推进这个大项目——建那些转运站。显然，我们本该能两件事都做。

turns.en: But so now what we're doing is after we completed this 70,000 block volumetric analysis, Can.
turns.zh: 但现在我们在做的是，在完成这项覆盖 70,000 个街区的体积分析之后……能……

turns.en: You say a little bit more about the analysis? Because I don't even know how you would start such a project. Because if you look at an apartment building, it's like, OK, maybe they produce like X pounds of waste on a certain day. But then the day after Christmas, that suddenly explodes and becomes five times as much.
turns.zh: ……你多讲讲这个分析吗？因为我甚至不知道这样的项目你从何下手。因为你看看一栋公寓楼，就是说，好吧，也许他们在某一天产生 X 磅的废物。但到了圣诞节后一天，那量突然爆炸，变成五倍。

turns.en: Yeah, absolutely.
turns.zh: 是啊，绝对。

turns.en: So when you look at one thing that I think is important to remember as we talk about this is that even though New York has a reputation for being behind the curve, there's actually no city in North America that does on-street containerization.
turns.zh: 所以当你看——我觉得在我们谈这个时，有一点很重要，值得记住：尽管纽约以落后于潮流著称，但实际上北美没有任何一座城市在做街边集装箱化。

turns.en: Right?
turns.zh: 对吧？

turns.en: It's a purely European, South American, and Asian thing. And when this program is implemented, New York will have gone, I would never say worse, but have gone from the back of the pack to first. And that means that we had to develop a system that would work for us specifically, right? As we first started to confront this, I heard a lot from sort of two groups, urbanists who would say, this is a solved problem, copy-paste Barcelona, copy-paste Amsterdam, and also community leaders in the city who said this would never work here, right? And when we did this study, what we really found was that both of those groups were wrong. It is, of course, achievable and it is.
turns.zh: 这纯粹是欧洲、南美和亚洲的做法。而当这个项目落地时，纽约将会——我绝不会说“更差”——从队伍的末尾跃居第一。这意味着我们必须专门为自己开发一套适用的系统，对吧？当我们刚开始面对这个问题时，我听到了两类人说的很多话：一类是城市规划主义者（urbanists），他们会说，这是个已经解决的问题，复制粘贴 Barcelona，复制粘贴 Amsterdam；另一类是本市的社区领袖，他们说这在这儿永远行不通，对吧？而当我们做了这项研究后，我们真正发现的是这两类人都错了。它当然是可以实现的，而且……

turns.en: Of course, difficult. So when we had all this.
turns.zh: ……当然，很难。所以当我们有了所有这些……

turns.en: Data about the weight of the trash, what we wanted to do was, again, as I mentioned, that there's a finite amount of street space. You want to establish a containerization model that can hold all the waste, but that is not oversized because then.
turns.zh: ……关于垃圾重量的数据后，我们想做的是——再说一次，正如我提到的——街道空间是有限的。你想建立一个集装箱化模式，既能装下所有废物，又不至于过大，因为那样……

turns.en: You're wasting that space.
turns.zh: ……你就是在浪费那块空间。

turns.en: So we planned for one extra day. You mentioned Christmas. And we planned for basically one extra day above their collection. And we went out and measured piles of trash. We eventually were able to come up with conversion formula to use. But it was a lot of on-the-street work measuring both the trash itself and also the streetscape. Because you might know the length of a block, but you know that you can't put the bin in front of a curb cut. You know it can't go in front of a fire hydrant. We had determined that we were going to go with a side-loading model. There are different ways the trucks can be serviced. That meant that we had to think about tree canopy height. The bin can't go up into the tree. There are so many factors in really four dimensions on this to consider. And in Europe in particular, what you see are open shared bins. And this is what had kind of been contemplated in earlier pilots that we had done going back to 2021-2022. okay, just a European style, basically a dumpster on the street that everybody on the block is to use. We always had a lot of issues with that as an at-scale solution because a few reasons. First of all, in New York City, we provide this free unlimited service for residents. Businesses have to pay for trash collection and through a network of private carters. And so there was a concern about, well, if it's a free open bin, why wouldn't a business just steal space in that bin.
turns.zh: 所以我们按多出的一天来规划。你提到了圣诞节。我们基本上是在他们收运量之上再多规划一天。我们实地出去测量一堆堆的垃圾。我们最终得出了一套可用的换算公式。但那是大量在街头实地做的工作，既要测垃圾本身，也要测街景。因为你也许知道一个街区的长度，但你知道你不能把垃圾箱放在路缘坡道（curb cut）前面。你知道它不能放在消防栓前面。我们已经确定要用侧装（side-loading）模式。卡车的装卸有不同的方式。那意味着我们必须考虑树冠高度。垃圾箱不能顶到树里去。要考虑的因素实在太多，简直是四个维度上的。而在欧洲，你看到的尤其是开放式的共享垃圾箱。这也正是我们在更早的试点里——回溯到 2021、2022 年——曾经设想过的模式。好，就用欧洲式的，基本上就是街上放一个大垃圾箱，整个街区的人都来用。作为一个大规模方案，我们对它一直有很多顾虑，原因有几个。首先，在纽约市，我们给居民提供这项免费、无限量的服务。商家则必须为垃圾收运付费，而且是通过一个由私营清运商（private carters）组成的网络。所以就有一种担忧：嗯，如果这是个免费开放的垃圾箱，商家为什么不干脆把垃圾塞进那个箱里蹭空间。

turns.en: With their trash in there?
turns.zh: 把他们的垃圾塞进去？

turns.en: So we didn't want to go forward with that model. We also knew that there are many neighborhoods in the city where an on-street container was not going to improve the situation. If you think about a low-density neighborhood, making everybody all of a sudden walk down to the middle of the block, that doesn't help just in the name of saying, well, we've done the whole city. So the model we eventually came up with after we had this volumetric data was a containerization system for low-density buildings, one to nine residential units, so a single-family home up through a small apartment. using a wheeled trash bin and then eventually a specific wheeled trash bin. The largest buildings, 31 or more units, is the point we came up with where they can certainly support at least one of what we call empire bins, the on-street containers. And then the 10 to 30s, the mid-sized buildings, was where we found there's a lot of variety. Might be 11 studios, there's 11 people in the building, versus 29 two-bedrooms. They have to use one or the other, but they choose.
turns.zh: 所以我们不想推进那个模式。我们还知道，城里有很多社区，街边集装箱并不能改善状况。你想一个低密度社区，让所有人突然都得走到街区中间去扔，这并没有帮助，只是为了能说“嗯，我们把全城都做了”。所以在我们拿到这些体积数据之后，最终得出的模式是：针对低密度建筑——1 到 9 个住宅单元，也就是从单户住宅到小型公寓——采用一套集装箱化系统，用带轮的垃圾桶，最终会是一款特定的带轮垃圾桶。而最大的建筑——31 个单元及以上——是我们得出的一个界限，它们当然能支撑至少一个我们称之为 Empire 箱（empire bins）的东西，也就是街边集装箱。然后 10 到 30 单元这个区间，那些中等规模的建筑，是我们发现差异很大的地方。可能有 11 个单间公寓（studio），也就是楼里 11 个人；相比之下也可能是 29 个两居室。他们必须二选一，但由他们自己选。

turns.en: And that program....
turns.zh: 而那个项目……

turns.en: With that model was implemented, the city's divided into 59 community districts. We began in one community district, Manhattan 9, which is West Harlem, Amsterdam to the river, 111 to 155 in June of last year, 2025. And now, fall 2026, this is coming to a second district, Brooklyn Community District 2, which is downtown Brooklyn through Fort Greene, Clinton Hill, Brooklyn Heights. That is the point that this really moves beyond a pilot and becomes a real program that New Yorkers can expect to see in their neighborhood. And the mayor has actually committed to funding this program for a full rollout by the end of 2031.
turns.zh: ……在那个模式下落地：全市被划分为 59 个社区区（community districts）。我们从一个社区区开始，Manhattan 9，也就是 West Harlem，从 Amsterdam 大道到河边，111 街到 155 街，是在去年 2025 年 6 月。而现在，2026 年秋天，它将来到第二个区，Brooklyn 社区 2 区，涵盖 downtown Brooklyn 一直到 Fort Greene、Clinton Hill、Brooklyn Heights。到了这个节点，它才真正超越试点，成为一个纽约人可以期待在自己社区看到的实在项目。而且市长其实已经承诺为这个项目拨款，以便在 2031 年底前全面铺开。

turns.en: I'm kind of curious, like, I actually don't know which, what I have right now.
turns.zh: 我有点好奇，就是，我其实不知道我现在用的是哪种。

turns.en: So what I have right now.
turns.zh: 就是我现在用的……

turns.en: In my- It's a damning indictment of how often you take out the trash.
turns.zh: 在我的——这真是个有力的控诉，说明你多久倒一次垃圾。

turns.en: No, I take out the trash every day. But like, so the way, like- You take it to a central location, right? No, no, no.
turns.zh: 不，我每天都倒垃圾。但就是，方式嘛，就是——你是把它拿到一个集中点，对吧？不不不。

turns.en: We have like this sort of like, I live in a building that's like four units. It's like fairly small in the East Village. And I don't just like put my trash out on the street. We have like this closed container and then I lift it up and then et cetera. Walk me through from the perspective of the sanitation worker. So what are they doing now to get that trash out of it? And then how will their day be different under the container? Like walk me through that when they're going down my block. What does it look like today and what does it look like when this is implemented?
turns.zh: 我们有那种，就是，我住的那栋楼大概四个单元。在 East Village，算是挺小的。我不是直接把垃圾扔到街上。我们有这么个封闭的容器，然后我把它掀开，等等。请从清洁工的视角带我们走一遍。那么他们现在是怎么把垃圾从里面弄出来的？然后在集装箱（模式）下，他们的一天会有什么不同？就带我们走一遍，当他们沿着我那个街区收的时候。今天是什么样，等这个落地后又是什么样？

turns.en: East Village is a great example because you'll have every kind of building within a single round there. So a sanitation worker is not servicing the container that you're describing.
turns.zh: East Village 是个很好的例子，因为你在那一趟里就能碰到各种类型的建筑。所以清洁工并不会去处理你描述的那个容器。

turns.en: It's like up against the building wall.
turns.zh: 它就是贴着建筑墙放的。

turns.en: Yeah, it's up against the building.
turns.zh: 对，是贴着楼的。

turns.en: Someone that your landlord is paying is coming and moving the material out.
turns.zh: 是你房东付钱雇的某个人过来，把物料搬出去。

turns.en: To the curb. That's actually one of the things that we were able to build it. Well, someone is coming and moving it out.
turns.zh: 搬到路边。这其实是我们能够把它建起来的原因之一。嗯，是有人过来把它搬出去。

turns.en: Our building hires this person.
turns.zh: 我们楼雇了这个人。

turns.en: In New York City- Most buildings are required to have a professional waste manager, someone who takes the trash out. And we wanted to maintain that system because they do a lot of things and.
turns.zh: 在纽约市——大多数建筑都被要求配备一名专业的废物管理员，也就是负责把垃圾拿出去的人。我们想保留这套体系，因为他们做很多事情，而且……

turns.en: Because it builds cleanliness in the neighborhood in general.
turns.zh: ……因为它总体上营造了社区的清洁。

turns.en: So right now, those bags are coming out of your sealed container.
turns.zh: 所以眼下，那些垃圾袋是从你的封闭容器里被拿出来的。

turns.en: They're going to the curb.
turns.zh: 它们被搬到路边。

turns.en: Sanitation workers are taking them out and putting them in the back. They should be going out because you have fewer than nine units in an official NYC bin. And if they are not, you are subject to a summons as.
turns.zh: 清洁工把它们收走、扔进车后斗。它们本应放在一个官方的 NYC 垃圾桶里出去，因为你的楼少于九个单元。如果没有，你就会收到一张传票，从……

turns.en: Of September of this year.
turns.zh: ……今年九月起。

turns.en: Let's slow down.
turns.zh: 我们慢一点说。

turns.en: But the trash is essentially not supposed to, from a building of your size, not supposed to sit on the ground directly anymore.
turns.zh: 但基本上，从你这种规模的楼里出来的垃圾，不应该再直接放在地上了。

turns.en: It never does, actually.
turns.zh: 其实它从来不直接放地上。

turns.en: So it goes out in a bin.
turns.zh: 所以它是放在桶里出去的。

turns.en: Sanitation workers can either tip the bin manually, or soon the trucks will have a rear tipper for the small buildings.
turns.zh: 清洁工既可以手动把桶倾倒进车，要么很快卡车就会配一个后部倾倒装置（rear tipper），用于那些小型建筑。

turns.en: Yeah, we have the real bins.
turns.zh: 对，我们有那种正规的桶。

turns.en: So they.
turns.zh: 所以他们……

turns.en: They have the bar on them. The bar hooks up to the rear tipper and it goes in the back. For the Empire bin, for larger buildings, we had to design an all new truck for this. I mentioned that New York City is the first place in North America to do on-street containerization. Once we studied rear loading versus side loading, container models, we came up with what we wanted to do. And we discovered that one of the long poles in the tent was going to be that there was no, what's called an automated side loader, ASL truck, that was appropriate for residential use in New York City. Like They have one that they use at the Port of Philadelphia. I saw this thing operate. It was so loud. The idea that it was going to come down your street was ludicrous. So we talked to some truck industry experts and heard that it would probably take about five years to design a truck from scratch. You can't just import the ones from Europe. There's different emission standards. We were not going to wait five years for that. So we actually got involved in the Department of Sanitation in the truck design business, something I knew nothing about going into this. And we learned how to do it. And we got a prototype truck built in about 10 months. And that's the truck that is now rolling off the line. It's operating in West Harlem. We're getting them in for the other districts going forward. So it's a combination of vendors. This is actually how we were able to do it so quickly. It's the European body, the side-loading body. And Mack makes the chassis exactly the same as they do for many of our current collection trucks.
turns.zh: 桶上有一根横杆。横杆挂到后部倾倒装置上，垃圾就进到车后斗。至于 Empire 箱，用于较大的建筑，我们不得不为它设计一款全新的卡车。我提到过，纽约市是北美第一个做街边集装箱化的地方。一旦我们研究了后装（rear loading）对比侧装（side loading）的集装箱模式，我们就想清楚要怎么做。然后我们发现，其中的一个“顶梁难题”（long pole in the tent）会是：没有一款所谓的自动化侧装车（automated side loader，ASL 卡车）适合在纽约市做住宅用途。比如 Philadelphia 港有一款他们在用的。我看过那玩意儿运作。它太吵了。想象它要开到你家街上来，太荒唐了。所以我们和一些卡车行业专家谈了谈，听说从零设计一款卡车大概要五年。你不能直接把欧洲的进口过来。排放标准不一样。我们可不打算为那个等五年。所以我们清洁局干脆自己下场干起了卡车设计这门生意——这是我接手时一无所知的领域。我们学会了怎么做。我们在大约 10 个月里造出了一款原型卡车。那就是现在正陆续下线的卡车。它已经在 West Harlem 运营。我们后续会给其他区陆续配备。所以这是多家供应商的组合。这其实正是我们能做得这么快的原因：用的是欧洲的车身，那个侧装车身；而 Mack 制造底盘，和他们为我们现有的很多收运卡车造的一模一样。

turns.en: And then we work with.
turns.zh: 然后我们和一家……合作。

turns.en: a firm that specializes in getting the two sets of electronics to talk to each other.
turns.zh: ……专门让两套电子系统相互“对话”的公司合作。

turns.en: And we've got.
turns.zh: 然后我们有……

turns.en: Probably about 20 of them operating now out of our full fleet of 2,300 or so, but they'll continue to come in as this program rolls out over the next.
turns.zh: ……大概 20 辆在运营，而我们整个车队大约有 2,300 辆；但随着这个项目在接下来……铺开，它们会持续到位。

turns.en: Five or six years.
turns.zh: ……五六年里。

turns.en: I want to go back to something you touched on earlier, which is deciding where the bins actually go, because this is a meaningful way in which the Department of Sanitation might actually change the look and feel of of New York. So when you're choosing where to put a bin, I mean, as you said, space is at a premium in New York and there's a bunch of other stuff that could go in that bin space. You could have a parking space being the obvious one or, I don't know, a space for deliveries or people to get in and out of taxi cabs, whatever. Talk a little bit more about the decision-making process for doing that and how you're judging the value of collecting trash versus other things.
turns.zh: 我想回到你早前提到的一点，就是决定垃圾箱到底放在哪儿，因为这是清洁局可能真正改变纽约面貌和气质的一种重要方式。所以当你在选择把垃圾箱放哪儿时，我是说，正如你讲的，纽约的空间寸土寸金，而那块能放垃圾箱的空间还能干一堆别的事。可以是一个停车位，这是最明显的；或者，我不知道，一个送货的位置，或者人们上下出租车的位置，诸如此类。多讲讲做这个决定的决策过程，以及你是如何衡量“收垃圾”相对于其他事情的价值的。

turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.en: One of the reasons that we were not interested in the European model of shared containers for the most part is because you then face this challenge of like, well, why is it in front of my house and not your house if it's for both of us? Under the model we came up with where larger buildings support their own bin, it's in front of your building. because it's for your building. So that eliminates a lot of the concerns about spatial jockeying. Okay, I live in a 50-unit building, we get an empire bin, and it goes right in.
turns.zh: 我们大体上对欧洲的共享集装箱模式不感兴趣，原因之一是：那样你就会面临这样的挑战——嗯，既然它是我们两家共用的，为什么它在我家门口而不在你家门口？在我们想出的这个模式下，较大的建筑自己配一个箱，它就放在你那栋楼前面，因为它是给你那栋楼用的。这就消除了很多关于“抢地盘”的顾虑。好，我住在一栋 50 单元的楼里，我们得到一个 Empire 箱，它就直接放在……

turns.en: Front of the building.
turns.zh: ……楼前面。

turns.en: And it's important to remember that while this is taking up curb space, it's freeing up sidewalk space where the bags are currently kept for collection. So you get that space back for pedestrians. We've also heard, especially in West Harlem, from quite a few supers and waste managers who say, I love that I don't have to keep it in the building anymore.
turns.zh: 而且要记住很重要的一点：尽管这占用了路缘空间，它却释放了人行道空间——那些垃圾袋目前就堆在人行道上等着被收。所以你把那块空间还给了行人。我们还听到，尤其是在 West Harlem，不少楼管（supers）和废物管理员说：“我太喜欢再也不用把它存在楼里了。”

turns.en: I just got.
turns.zh: 我刚……

turns.en: 30 to 50 square feet of building space back without any new additional construction because where I used to put the trash, it can now go straight into the bin outside.
turns.zh: ……白白拿回了 30 到 50 平方英尺的楼内空间，没有任何新增建设，因为我原来放垃圾的地方，现在垃圾可以直接进外面的箱子。

turns.en: That said, the street layout issues are huge.
turns.zh: 话虽如此，街道布局的问题非常大。

turns.en: And we work very closely with the City Department of Transportation on coordinating around some of the things that I mentioned, you know, hydrants, curb cuts. We don't take designated handicap spaces. We've also in BK2, the second district that's coming online, we were interested in piloting shared containers within our locked model. by buildings that opt in to share. So we said, you know, two small buildings decide they don't qualify on their own, but they.
turns.zh: 我们和城市交通局（Department of Transportation）就我提到的一些事项密切协作，你知道的，消防栓、路缘坡道。我们不占用指定的残障人士车位。而且在 BK2——就是即将上线的第二个区——我们很有兴趣在我们的锁定模式下试点共享集装箱，由那些自愿加入共享的建筑来做。所以我们说，你知道的，两栋小楼觉得自己单独不够格，但他们……

turns.en: Want to share one.
turns.zh: ……想共用一个。

turns.en: And that actually really exposed some of the street limitations. There were a handful of buildings that were interested and they were on streets with full no parking, no place to put them. So it's something we'll continue to explore in future zones. But absolutely, you know, we think that the initial, what we call the future of trash report back in spring of 22, where we sort of first began to.
turns.zh: 而那实际上真的暴露了街道的一些局限。有那么几栋楼有兴趣，但它们在完全禁停的街上，没地方放。所以这是我们在未来的片区里会继续探索的事。但当然，你知道的，我们认为最初那份——我们称之为“垃圾的未来”（future of trash）报告，在 22 年春天，那时我们大致第一次开始……

turns.en: Look at the feasibility of this in a meaningful way.
turns.zh: ……以有意义的方式审视这件事的可行性。

turns.en: Said that on-street containerization could take up to 150,000 parking spaces. Now, that was before we had gotten into, and that's out of 3 million total in the city. That was before we had gotten into some of the details. Once we had analyzed it much further and gone down the road on implementation, we're now looking at about a fifth of that. When we went back and did the Back to the Future of Trash report, we found that it was more like 30,000 spaces at full rollout, and it could be fewer based on the opt-ins.
turns.zh: ……报告说街边集装箱化最多可能占用 150,000 个停车位。那可是——这还没算全市总共 300 万个车位里的一部分。那是在我们深入一些细节之前。一旦我们做了更深入的分析和实施推进，我们现在看到的大约是那个数的五分之一。当我们回头做了“重回垃圾的未来”（Back to the Future of Trash）报告时，我们发现全面铺开后更像是 30,000 个车位，而且根据自愿加入的情况，可能更少。

turns.en: Can we just talk a little bit more about the perspective of the sanitation workers? So first of all, how many are on a truck right now?
turns.zh: 我们能再多聊聊清洁工这个视角吗？首先，现在一辆车上有几个人？

turns.en: Two. There's two people on a truck.
turns.zh: 两个。一辆车上两个人。

turns.en: Currently. Yes.
turns.zh: 目前是。对。

turns.en: And it will still be two under the new- That's correct.
turns.zh: 而在新的（模式）下仍然是两个——没错。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And how does.
Their walk me through literally what they physically do? They go and collect it, et cetera. How does it look different now or future versus now?
turns.zh: ……他们，具体带我们走一遍他们实际做什么？他们去收垃圾等等。未来和现在相比看起来有什么不同？

turns.en: Yes. So sanitation workers have an incredibly difficult job. They're out there collecting 12 to 13 tons of trash in- all weather, in all conditions. They can't say, you know, I couldn't get to it today, right? There's an expectation that it'll be gone. And about 50% of their line of duty injuries are sprains and strains from throwing bags. So we're excited to see that go away. There are about 6,500 people with the title of sanitation worker out of 10,000 people total at the department. So those are the people who are actually collecting and processing your trash. They are subject to a number of hazards on the job. One thing we've seen a big increase is being poked by needles. We assume it's from an increase in GLP-1 usage with people.
turns.zh: 对。清洁工的工作极其艰难。他们要在各种天气、各种条件下外出收运 12 到 13 吨垃圾。他们不能说，你知道的，“我今天没顾上”，对吧？大家期待垃圾会被清走。他们执勤受伤中大约 50% 是扔袋子造成的扭伤和拉伤。所以我们很高兴看到这种情况消失。全部门一共 10,000 人，其中约 6,500 人的头衔是清洁工。所以他们就是真正在收运和处理你垃圾的人。他们在工作中面临多种危害。我们看到大幅增加的一件事，是被针头扎到。我们推测这是因为人们使用 GLP-1（减肥药）的增加。

turns.en: Buying them online.
turns.zh: 在网上买的那种。

turns.en: And it comes with an instruction booklet, but they don't necessarily read it because it came from an online pharmacy and whatever. And then they think, this is trash. I put it in the bag and it goes away. And so a big thing that we want people to remember, of course, is a human being handles your garbage. But the move to mechanized collection, the side-loading truck, in high density areas will make a huge difference for the backs and knees of sanitation workers. They go out, they begin their day with a roll call at their garage. I mentioned the city's divided into 59 districts. They start at one of their assigned district. They do a roll call, they get their assignment for the day.
turns.zh: 它随附一本说明书，但他们不一定会读，因为它是从网上药房买的之类的。然后他们就想，这是垃圾。我把它扔进袋子，它就消失了。所以我们希望大家记住的一件大事，当然是：是活生生的人在处理你的垃圾。但在高密度地区转向机械化收运——那款侧装卡车——将对清洁工的背部和膝盖带来巨大改变。他们出勤，一天从在车场点名开始。我提到全市分为 59 个区。他们在被指派的某个区开始。他们点名，领取当天的任务。

turns.en: There's a big.
turns.zh: 有一块大……

turns.en: Electronic board where they find out where they're working that day. They go out with their partner and they collect the trash. And then in many, but not all districts, they get to dump it at the transfer station on the same shift. Some districts where the routes are optimized differently, it's another shift comes in and empties the truck so that it's empty when people come back.
turns.zh: ……电子板，他们在那儿看到当天要在哪儿干活。他们和搭档一起出车收垃圾。然后在很多区（但不是所有区），他们能在同一个班次里就把垃圾卸到转运站。有些区的路线优化方式不同，是另一个班次进来把车清空，这样人们回来时车是空的。

turns.en: In the morning.
turns.zh: 早上回来时。

turns.en: These are people who deal with every possible situation you can imagine. And if we can get it so that they are not lifting your garbage as much, it will.
turns.zh: 这些人要应对你能想象到的每一种情况。如果我们能做到让他们不用那么频繁地抬你的垃圾，那将会……

turns.en: Make a huge difference.
turns.zh: ……带来巨大改变。

turns.en: What happens to bulky waste under the new system?
turns.zh: 在新体系下，大件垃圾（bulky waste）怎么处理？

turns.en: Because one of the nice things about New York City right now is, you know, you can put a couch on a curb, and sometimes people will just take it and use it on their own. But if they don't, then the trash collectors will come and they'll throw it away and you don't have to pay extra.
turns.zh: 因为纽约市眼下的一件好事是，你知道的，你可以把一张沙发放到路边，有时候人们就直接拿走自己用了。但如果没人拿，收垃圾的人就会来把它扔掉，而你不用额外付钱。

turns.en: To do that.
turns.zh: 来做这事。

turns.en: Yeah, no change.
turns.zh: 对，没有变化。

turns.en: If there's an item that doesn't fit in your bin, you know, a couch is a great example, just leave it next to it. A truck will still be coming down. We hope to find efficiencies at full rollout and have to run fewer of the trucks, the rear loader, the sort of traditional collection truck that can get bulky items. But that was actually one of the things we learned from Barcelona. Barcelona is often held up as the gold standard of waste management in urban environment. We talked to them at the beginning of this process and asked them quite a few questions about what worked and also what they would have done differently. And it was interesting because American urbanists will tell you.
turns.zh: 如果有什么东西放不进你的桶里，你知道的，沙发就是个很好的例子，就把它放在桶旁边。仍然会有卡车开来。我们希望在全面铺开后找到效率，从而少跑一些那种后装车——就是那种能装大件物品的传统收运车。但这其实正是我们从 Barcelona 学到的东西之一。Barcelona 常被誉为城市环境废物管理的黄金标准。我们在这个过程一开始就和他们谈过，问了不少问题：什么奏效，以及有什么他们会做得不一样。这很有意思，因为美国的规划主义者会告诉你……

turns.en: That Barcelona is perfect, we should just do Barcelona.
turns.zh: ……Barcelona 是完美的，我们就该照搬 Barcelona。

turns.en: And the Barcelona people were like, we still have a lot of issues. One of which was that they had converted their fleet too heavily to sideloaders. And then learned, well, actually, people still put a loose bag next to it once in a while. They still need the couch. And they had to go back and get a different truck. So we're making sure to keep that as part of the program.
turns.zh: 而 Barcelona 那边的人却说：“我们还有很多问题。”其中之一就是他们把车队过度地转成了侧装车。然后他们发现，嗯，其实人们偶尔还是会在旁边扔一个散袋子。他们还是需要处理沙发。于是他们不得不回头再搞一种不同的卡车。所以我们确保把这一点保留在项目里。

turns.en: Just out of curiosity, in this international exploration, did you ever look into Mexico City? Because I've never been to a city that's, A, more clean. And, B, you can't find a trash can for the life of you. And I'm like, where do people put their, like, you buy something from a street food vendor.
turns.zh: 纯粹好奇，在这场国际考察中，你有没有研究过 Mexico City？因为我从没去过一座城市，一是更干净，二是你死活找不到一个垃圾桶。我就想，人们把他们的……比如你从街头小吃摊买了点东西。

turns.en: You have this wrapper. And I'm like, I don't know where to throw it away. There's no trash cans anywhere. And yet the streets are spotless. I don't get it. You know, public space.
turns.zh: 你手上有个包装纸。我就想，我不知道该扔哪儿。到处都没有垃圾桶。可街道却一尘不染。我搞不懂。你知道的，公共空间。

turns.en: Litter baskets and public space maintenance are different across the world. And we have talked to them. And, you know, we have responsibility here for the property owner to maintain the sidewalk. In Mexico City and in Tokyo, which is the other sort of famously clean streetscape city, there are community groups who are paid or tasked with maintenance. And we have that as well through the business improvement districts system. We did in 2018 conduct a one-district pilot where we tried going with the Tokyo-Mexico City model and removed every litter basket. Because people sometimes say, oh, the litter baskets, they attract the trash.
turns.zh: 废纸篓（litter baskets）和公共空间维护在世界各地各不相同。我们也和他们谈过。你知道的，我们这儿是由业主负责维护人行道。在 Mexico City 和 Tokyo——后者是另一座以街景干净闻名的城市——有一些社区团体受雇或受托来做维护。我们也通过商业改良区（business improvement districts）体系有这种做法。我们确实在 2018 年做过一个单区试点，尝试走 Tokyo-Mexico City 模式，把每一个废纸篓都撤掉了。因为人们有时会说，哦，那些废纸篓，它们会招垃圾。

turns.en: People littered everywhere.
turns.zh: 结果人们到处乱扔。

turns.en: So that said, I don't want to preclude for your future study. It is true that piles of trash attract additional trash. And when you're in a neighborhood that is not containerized and you see a pile of black bags, it is natural to think, I can put my garbage on top of this. So my hope is that after full containerization, we can reevaluate some of that further and say, OK, now that the city broadly doesn't have trash.
turns.zh: 话虽如此，我不想为你未来的研究下结论。确实，成堆的垃圾会招来更多垃圾。当你身处一个还没集装箱化的社区、看到一堆黑袋子时，很自然地会想：我可以把我的垃圾扔在这堆上面。所以我的希望是，在全面集装箱化之后，我们能进一步重新评估这一点，然后说：好，既然整座城市大体上都没有垃圾……

turns.en: Everywhere, what can we do to limit littering and public space cleanliness issues?
turns.zh: ……到处都没有了，那我们能做些什么来限制乱扔垃圾和公共空间清洁的问题？

turns.en: This is a slightly random question, but what happened to the anti-littering campaigns of like the 80s and 90s, I guess as far back as the 70s? Because I feel like you just don't see them as much anymore. And it's not like, I don't.
turns.zh: 这是个有点跳脱的问题，但那些 80、90 年代——我想最早能追到 70 年代——的反乱扔垃圾宣传去哪儿了？因为我觉得你就是不太看得到了。而且也不是说，我不……

turns.en: Think you can look at New York and say, mission accomplished. There's no more littering.
turns.zh: ……觉得你能看着纽约说“任务完成”。不再有乱扔垃圾了。

turns.en: I totally agree.
turns.zh: 我完全同意。

turns.en: I will say that I do think that there's some confirmation bias and selective memory about these because we... Ran a multi-million dollar one last year, the We Heart NYC anti-littering campaign. We ran one that was well into the six figures recently that had a picture of a finger pointing up into an NYC litter basket and said, if you see someone littering, tell them where to stick it.
turns.zh: 我要说的是，我确实认为对这些宣传存在一些确认偏误（confirmation bias）和选择性记忆，因为我们……去年就搞了一个耗资数百万美元的，那个“We Heart NYC”反乱扔垃圾宣传。我们最近还搞了一个花费高达六位数的，上面画着一根手指指向一个 NYC 废纸篓，写着：“如果你看到有人乱扔垃圾，告诉他们该把它塞哪儿。”

turns.en: We ran a few of these.
turns.zh: 我们搞过好几个这样的。

turns.en: And the issue is, I think, probably the same one that you find across the media landscape, right? The monoculture is long over. And we try to do a tremendous amount.
turns.zh: 而问题在于，我觉得，大概和你在整个媒体版图上看到的是同一个，对吧？单一文化（monoculture）早就结束了。而我们尝试做大量的……

turns.en: Of littering outreach.
turns.zh: ……反乱扔垃圾的宣传推广。

turns.en: But, you know, this came up a lot in January, February.
turns.zh: 但你知道的，这在 1 月、2 月被反复提起。

turns.en: This year when there was a sort of persistent dog waste issue.
turns.zh: 今年，当时有一个持续存在的狗粪便问题。

turns.en: Oh, yeah. And I would often remind people that as frustrating as it is and as much as we do want to and are planning to do more, there is no one in the city who doesn't clean up after their dog because.
turns.zh: 哦，是的。我常常会提醒人们，尽管这很令人沮丧，尽管我们确实想做、也计划做更多，但这城里没有谁不清理自己狗的粪便，是因为……

turns.en: They don't know the rules, right?
turns.zh: ……他们不知道规则，对吧？

turns.en: Of course, you know, outreach and education is great, but it's not like they go, oh, yeah, you know, I didn't know you had to clean up after your dog and now I saw the ad.
turns.zh: 当然，你知道的，宣传推广和教育很好，但并不是说他们会“哦，是啊，你知道吗，我原来不知道得清理狗粪，现在我看到了那个广告（所以改了）”。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: We do them.
turns.zh: 我们会做这些。

turns.en: Every sanitation truck comes with a poster space on the side. We put anti-littering messages on those posters frequently. We've had longstanding relationships with the arts community. You've probably seen the early 90s David Lynch anti-littering ad that he did with the SNY. It's something that we're interested in, but also I do think that we're at the point where we see the built environment as the bigger issue here. And I'll bring it back to some of the philosophy behind this. One of the thinkers who informed a lot of the work of the trash revolution that really gets at what you're talking about is a 70s urban planner named Oscar Newman, who wrote a book called Defensible Space that was basically what he did in the book was he said that controlling even for income, for age, for all demographics, He found that public housing still had, at that time, a higher rate of crime than market rate housing.
turns.zh: 每辆清洁车侧面都有一块海报位。我们经常在上面放反乱扔垃圾的信息。我们和艺术界有着长期的合作关系。你大概见过 90 年代初 David Lynch 为 DSNY 做的那支反乱扔垃圾广告。这是我们感兴趣的，但我也确实认为，我们已经到了把建成环境（built environment）看作这里更大问题的阶段。我要把它拉回到这背后的一些哲学。有一位思想家为“垃圾革命”的很多工作提供了养分，也真正切中了你在谈的东西，他是 70 年代一位名叫 Oscar Newman 的城市规划师，写了一本叫《可防御空间》（Defensible Space）的书。他在书里基本做的是：他说，即便控制了收入、年龄、所有人口统计变量，他发现公共住房在当时仍然比市场价住房有更高的犯罪率。

turns.en: And so what was the cause?
turns.zh: 那么原因是什么？

turns.en: And he proposed that there were elements of the design of the space that caused this issue, specifically that there were significant parts of many urban public housing developments that didn't feel like they belonged to anyone.
turns.zh: 他提出，是空间设计中的一些元素导致了这个问题，具体来说，很多城市公共住房项目中有相当大的一部分，让人感觉不属于任何人。

turns.en: They were everyone's.
turns.zh: 它们属于所有人。

turns.en: Oh, yeah.
turns.zh: 哦，是啊。

turns.en: And so he proposed....
turns.zh: 于是他提出了……

turns.en: A design model that would be did. So the most famous example of his design is the Yonkers row houses that were the subject of Lisa Belkin's book, Show Me a Hero, that won her the Pulitzer, I guess.
turns.zh: ……一种（能奏效的）设计模式。他设计最有名的例子就是 Yonkers 的联排住宅（row houses），那正是 Lisa Belkin 的书《Show Me a Hero》的主题，我想那本书为她赢得了普利策奖。

turns.en: In the late 90s.
turns.zh: 在 90 年代末。

turns.en: A big part of what we were thinking with this was how do we apply that same finding about crime to cleanliness? What do we do that makes it so that every part of the city.
turns.zh: 我们在这上面思考的一大块是：我们如何把那个关于犯罪的发现同样应用到清洁上？我们该做什么，才能让城市的每一部分……

turns.en: Belongs to someone?
turns.zh: ……都属于某个人？

turns.en: So that cleanliness is not just about trash removal, but about real care for public spaces. That's one of the reasons why the Empire bins are assigned to a specific building rather than shared. It's one of the reasons that we have done a lot of sort of continued expansion of the property owners are required to clean 18 inches into the street, that we've done a lot of work on that, that we have been so focused on expanding the ways in which we enforce alternate side parking, street sweeping regulations, because there should be no part of the city where someone can litter or someone can observe someone else litter and think that is not my fault. And the design that Newman put into place has been broadly seen as effective. And we're hopeful that over the next five or so years, we'll see those same design elements work on the cleanliness space.
turns.zh: ……从而清洁不只是清除垃圾，而是对公共空间真正的爱护。这正是 Empire 箱被指派给特定建筑、而非共享的原因之一。这也是我们持续大量扩展“业主须清扫向街内延伸 18 英寸的范围”的原因之一——我们在这上面做了很多工作；也是为什么我们如此专注于扩展我们执行“隔边停车”（alternate side parking）、扫街规定的方式——因为城市的任何一部分都不该出现这种情况：有人可以乱扔垃圾，或者有人看到别人乱扔垃圾却觉得“那不是我的错”。Newman 落地的那套设计被广泛认为是有效的。我们希望在接下来大约五年里，能看到同样的设计元素在清洁领域奏效。

turns.en: Tracy, is it well known that don't mess with Texas, that phrase you hear a lot, was an anti-littering thing?
turns.zh: Tracy，“别惹德州”（don't mess with Texas）这句你常听到的话，它其实是个反乱扔垃圾的宣传，这事广为人知吗？

turns.en: I know about it because my dad's Texan. I lived in Dallas.
turns.zh: 我知道这个，因为我爸是德州人。我在 Dallas 住过。

turns.en: Now everyone, don't mess with Texas, and people think it's some.
turns.zh: 现在人人都说“别惹德州”，人们以为它是某种……

turns.en: Sort of political thing.
turns.zh: ……政治性的东西。

turns.en: But it literally is just, and it still is.
turns.zh: 但它其实就是，而且现在仍然是……

turns.en: No, I mean, some of the anti-littering campaigns. Exactly. But to your point, I.
turns.zh: 不，我是说，一些反乱扔垃圾的宣传。正是。但说到你这点，我……

turns.en: Mean, this is also the problem with public shaming, by the way. If you see someone littering, they probably know what they're doing is bad, and so pointing out to someone who's doing a bad thing that what they're doing is bad is a little bit risky in New York sometimes.
turns.zh: ……我是说，顺便讲，这也是公开羞辱（public shaming）的问题所在。如果你看到有人乱扔垃圾，他们大概知道自己在做坏事，所以对一个正在做坏事的人指出他在做坏事，在纽约有时候是有点风险的。

turns.en: It could be, yeah. I'm still, I'm pro, I think I'm pro-shaming.
turns.zh: 可能吧，是的。我仍然，我支持，我想我是支持羞辱这一套的。

turns.en: I'm pro-public shaming, but that's different from saying that, like, I'm comfortable doing it constantly.
turns.zh: 我支持公开羞辱，但这跟说“我乐意随时都这么干”是两回事。

turns.en: We don't think of anything we do as shaming. We just want people to know, if you are someone who cares about your neighborhood, you are not alone. You are actually, in the majority, not the person littering.
turns.zh: 我们不把我们做的任何事看作羞辱。我们只是想让人们知道：如果你是那个在乎自己社区的人，你并不孤单。实际上，你属于多数，而不是那个乱扔垃圾的人。

turns.en: Can you talk a little bit about, you mentioned, okay, This containerization, it's in West Harlem. It's about to be in Brooklyn. So that's two of 59.
turns.zh: 你能不能稍微讲讲，你提到了，好，这个集装箱化，它在 West Harlem。它马上要到 Brooklyn。所以那是 59 个里的 2 个。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And it will start going much faster.
turns.zh: 而且它会开始快得多。

turns.en: What is the roadmap?
turns.zh: 路线图是怎样的？

turns.en: And you said the mayor is committed to funding it through. Does that mean it's not guaranteed currently that it will be rolled out to the entire city?
turns.zh: 你还说市长承诺为它拨款到位。那是不是意味着目前它并不保证会在全市铺开？

turns.en: No, it's guaranteed.
turns.zh: 不，是有保证的。

turns.en: I mean, we do annual budget cycles here. So the money's not literally there. But the commitment is as good as it gets to roll this out. And we've got strong support from the city council on this, too.
turns.zh: 我是说，我们这儿是年度预算周期。所以钱并不是实打实已经在那儿了。但要推进这件事，这份承诺已经是最靠谱的了。而且市议会（city council）在这件事上也给了我们强有力的支持。

turns.en: You know, it's funny. When we first started this, we heard a lot.
turns.zh: 你知道的，很有意思。我们刚开始做这个的时候，听到很多……

turns.en: Of concerns about pushback, and those concerns were mostly conceptual. I bet people will be mad about parking.
turns.zh: ……对阻力（pushback）的担忧，而那些担忧大多是概念层面的。“我打赌人们会为停车的事生气。”

turns.en: We heard that a lot.
turns.zh: 这话我们听得多了。

turns.en: Very few people are actually mad about parking, but we heard a lot. I bet people are going to push back. So as far as the rollout, It took, you know, 50 years to do the first district, another year to do the second, but we're going to do the remaining 57 in about five years as trucks start.
turns.zh: 真正为停车生气的人很少，但我们听了很多“我打赌人们会抵制”。所以至于铺开进度——你知道，做第一个区花了 50 年，做第二个区又花了一年，但剩下的 57 个区我们将在大约五年内完成，随着卡车开始……

turns.en: Rolling off the line.
turns.zh: ……陆续下线。

turns.en: Can you talk a little bit more about, you know, as you concede it to one fact, which is that you can't just copy and paste any other city's model onto New York City. So it's not, you know, even if containerization, et cetera, works, it's a little different. We might not have alleys. That's a difference. We might, whatever, every city is a little bit different. But then, as you mentioned, people can take a little bit too far and convince themselves that New York is just different. Yes, it looks like you can have, and then people really get dug in, and they come up with stories. Where does this impulse come from? That all around, you look at trash, and you have, like, there was an article in The New Yorker about, like, a trash anthropologist, and there was some quote that's like, oh, you don't understand New York.
turns.zh: 你能不能再多讲讲，你知道的，你承认了一个事实，就是你不能把任何其他城市的模式直接复制粘贴到纽约市。所以并不是说，你知道的，即便集装箱化等等行得通，它也略有不同。我们可能没有后巷。这是个差别。我们可能，反正每座城市都略有不同。但然后，正如你提到的，人们可能有点走过头，说服自己纽约就是不一样。是的，看起来你本可以有（干净的街道），然后人们就真的钻牛角尖，编出各种说法。这种冲动从何而来？就是那种，你环顾垃圾，然后你有——比如《New Yorker》上有篇文章讲一个“垃圾人类学家”，里面有句什么话，像是“哦，你不懂纽约”。

turns.en: Is it really a city?
turns.zh: “它真的算一座城市吗？”

turns.en: It's a series of sub-societies and blah, blah, blah, and it's just not like other cities, and that's why it doesn't work. Where does this impulse come from? This sort of, I would call it like an anti-New York exceptionalism.
turns.zh: “它是一连串的子社会”blah blah blah，“它就是不像其他城市，所以这套在这儿行不通。”这种冲动从何而来？这种——我会称之为一种“反纽约例外论”（anti-New York exceptionalism）。

turns.en: We just can't. There's something fundamental. We just can't have clean.
turns.zh: “我们就是做不到。有某种根本性的东西。我们就是没法拥有干净。”

turns.en: I don't even think it's anti-New York exceptionalism. I think it's just a different manifestation of the same New York exceptionalism. Our trash is special in some ways. You know, our bags are a beautiful part of our landscape. And of course they're not. And the waste stream has changed many times before, you know. One of the impetuses for the creation of the Department of Sanitation in the first place was that in the mid to late 19th century, there were dead horses all over the city and nobody whose job it was to pick them up. And then throughout the early 20th century, many buildings had in-building incinerators. The primary waste stream that we picked up was piles of ash. And then that moved to solid waste and we had the landfill model. This stuff has changed many times before. And I think it's the same nostalgic impulse that you see, like, you know, why every movie is a sequel, you know, because people want what they grew up with. And I think one of the big things we're trying to do is remind people that what you should be proud of is what's under the trash. Right.
turns.zh: 我甚至不觉得这是“反纽约例外论”。我觉得它只是同一种“纽约例外论”的另一种表现。“我们的垃圾在某些方面很特别。”你知道的，“我们的垃圾袋是我们城市景观中美丽的一部分。”当然它们不是。而废物流以前已经改变过很多次了，你知道的。最初促成清洁局成立的一个诱因，就是 19 世纪中后期，全城到处是死马，却没有谁的职责是把它们清走。然后在整个 20 世纪初，很多建筑里有楼内焚化炉。我们收运的主要废物流是一堆堆的灰烬。后来那变成了固体废物，我们有了填埋场模式。这些东西以前已经变过很多次了。我觉得这就是你在别处也看到的同一种怀旧冲动，比如你知道的，为什么每部电影都是续集，因为人们想要他们成长中所熟悉的东西。而我觉得我们试图做的大事之一，就是提醒人们：你真正该为之自豪的，是垃圾底下的东西。对吧。

turns.en: It's not.
turns.zh: 它不是……

turns.en: And, you know, we've we've done this a lot of different ways over the years.
turns.zh: 而且你知道的，这些年来我们已经用很多不同的方式做过这件事。

turns.en: I'm sorry.
turns.zh: 抱歉。

turns.en: Did you say what's under the trash?
turns.zh: 你刚说的是“垃圾底下的东西”？

turns.en: Sure.
turns.zh: 当然。

turns.en: The streets, the people, you know, we have an artist that we've worked with for many decades. Meryl Aderman Euclid did in the early 80s designed. a collection truck that's fully mirrored on the side. And the idea is called the social mirror.
turns.zh: 街道，人，你知道的，有一位艺术家我们合作了很多年。Meryl Aderman（Euclid）在 80 年代初设计了……一辆侧面完全镶镜的收运车。这个创意叫“社会之镜”（the social mirror）。

turns.en: It's a great piece.
turns.zh: 那是件很棒的作品。

turns.en: And it was intended to remind people, I make the trash. When I see the trash, that's me.
turns.zh: 它意在提醒人们：垃圾是我制造的。当我看到垃圾，那就是我。

turns.en: And unfortunately, we.
turns.zh: 而不幸的是，我们……

turns.en: Bring it out to parades now and people go, oh, it's the selfie truck. It's not the selfie truck. It's the truck with a deeper meaning behind it. But to your point about reproducibility and differences, the trash in New York, takes on sort of unique logistical space. We don't have the alleyways, we produce certain volumes, our density, but many cities face different challenges in the trash space and in other infrastructural areas. And I know a lot of them are looking at that now. Voters in Los Angeles have a ballot measure this year that would substantially rethink their structure of their public works agencies. I know Portland, Oregon just reorganized its city fleet asset management, D.C., eliminated the deputy mayor for operations two years ago and is now rethinking that decision.
turns.zh: ……现在把它开到游行上，人们就说：“哦，那是自拍卡车。”它不是自拍卡车。它是一辆背后有更深层含义的卡车。但说到你讲的“可复制性”和“差异”，纽约的垃圾确实占据了一种独特的后勤空间。我们没有后巷，我们产生一定的量，我们的密度——但很多城市在垃圾领域和其他基础设施领域面临不同的挑战。而且我知道其中很多城市现在正在审视这一点。Los Angeles 的选民今年有一项公投议案（ballot measure），将大幅重新思考他们公共工程机构的架构。我知道 Oregon 的 Portland 刚重组了它的城市车队资产管理；D.C. 两年前取消了负责运营的副市长一职，现在正在重新思考那个决定。

turns.en: So, you know, these are the questions, right?
turns.zh: 所以你知道的，这些才是问题所在，对吧？

turns.en: It's not so much necessarily about what do you do with the trash, but what do you do to say the way I've lived for 50 years is not the only way to live, right? That, you know, just as activists in this country look and say, you know.
turns.zh: 这与其说必然是关于“你怎么处理垃圾”，不如说是关于“你怎么去说出：我过了 50 年的那种生活方式，并不是唯一的生活方式”，对吧？就是，你知道的，就像这个国家的活动人士看着然后说，你知道的……

turns.en: Well, you know, they have this here. I want that.
turns.zh: “嗯，你知道的，他们这儿有这个。我也想要那个。”

turns.en: You know, we can have what every place has. Everyone can have a standard of living that they deserve. even as you make the trash and even as you expect someone else to just make it go away, there is more that you can do as a resident to sort of encourage responsible design.
turns.zh: 你知道的，我们可以拥有每个地方都有的东西。每个人都能拥有他们应得的生活水准。即便你制造垃圾、即便你指望别人干脆把它变没，作为一个居民，你还能做更多，去鼓励一种负责任的设计。

turns.en: Around this stuff.
turns.zh: 围绕这些东西（的设计）。

turns.en: Setting the New York exceptionalism argument aside for one second and setting all of New York aside, do you have a favorite trash collection system internationally? Like, what's your platonic ideal of a trash collection system?
turns.zh: 先把“纽约例外论”这个论调放一边，也把整个纽约放一边，你在国际上有没有一个最喜爱的垃圾收运系统？就是，你心目中垃圾收运系统的“柏拉图式理想”（platonic ideal）是什么样的？

turns.en: So there are a couple of places that had the opportunity to build them sort of from scratch. I wouldn't call them the platonic ideal because I'm very aware that these are not replicable models. But Singapore, which did a tremendous amount of greenfield development and was able to sort of put best practices in place from the beginning. And also Amsterdam, which was in a similar situation in the post-war era of being able to kind of restart a lot of their public space design. They use underground trash containers, had some advantages that I wish we would have had. You know, one of the things we learned in this process really surprised me was that there's actually no map of what's underneath the streets in New York. There's no one, you know, Con Ed knows where their stuff is and the subway knows where their stuff is. But there is not one master what we started calling the underground spaghetti.
turns.zh: 有那么几个地方曾有机会几乎从零开始建设。我不会称它们为柏拉图式理想，因为我很清楚这些并不是可复制的模式。但 Singapore 做了大量的“绿地开发”（greenfield development），得以从一开始就把最佳实践落地。还有 Amsterdam，它在战后时期处于类似的境地，能够某种程度重启它的很多公共空间设计。它们用地下垃圾集装箱，拥有一些我真希望我们也有的优势。你知道的，我们在这个过程中学到的一件事真的让我惊讶：纽约街道底下到底有什么，其实根本没有一张地图。没有一张，你知道的，Con Ed 知道他们的东西在哪儿，地铁知道他们的东西在哪儿。但没有一张总图，来标示我们开始称之为“地下意大利面”（underground spaghetti）的那些东西。

turns.en: All the guys who've been caught on camera coming out of the subway or out of the sewer system, they're.
turns.zh: 所有那些被拍到从地铁里或下水道系统里钻出来的人，他们都……

turns.en: Just, they're trying to map it, right?
turns.zh: 只是，他们在试图把它画成地图，对吧？

turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，正是。

turns.en: They're trying to figure out what's there.
turns.zh: 他们在试图搞清楚那底下有什么。

turns.en: You know, and my hope is that that will change. And, you know, I love the fact that in Tokyo, they have seven waste streams, whereas we've just gone from three to four. They separate so many more types of material. There are things that we could take from all over the world. But I think that the biggest thing that I hope that we continue to take is just a willingness to change.
turns.zh: 你知道的，我的希望是这一点会改变。而且你知道的，我很喜欢一个事实：在 Tokyo，他们有七个废物流，而我们刚从三个变到四个。他们分出的物料种类多得多。有些东西我们可以从全世界各地借鉴。但我觉得我最希望我们持续借鉴的最大一点，就是一种改变的意愿。

turns.en: By the way, if anyone's listening to this episode, you should watch it on YouTube because our guest here has a really cool jacket that I'm very jealous of. And I'm always jealous of Zoran's jackets, too.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，如果有人在听这一期，你应该去 YouTube 上看，因为我们这位嘉宾有一件超酷的夹克，我很眼馋。而且我也总是眼馋 Zoran 的夹克。

turns.en: He's got one of these.
turns.zh: 他有那种夹克之一。

turns.en: Yeah, I'm sure he does. And every time I see one of these press conferences, it's.
turns.zh: 是啊，我肯定他有。而且每次我看到这种新闻发布会，就是……

turns.en: You know, it's autumn in New York.
turns.zh: 你知道的，纽约的秋天。

turns.en: No matter how cool you think your jacket is, somebody has a cooler jacket.
turns.zh: 不管你觉得自己的夹克多酷，总有人有一件更酷的。

turns.en: So it's just part of the job.
turns.zh: 所以这只是工作的一部分。

turns.en: Josh Goodman, thank you so much for coming on All Thoughts.
turns.zh: Josh Goodman，非常感谢你来做客 Odd Lots。

turns.en: Really appreciate it.
turns.zh: 真的很感谢。

turns.en: It was my pleasure. Thank you both so much. And don't litter.
turns.zh: 这是我的荣幸。非常感谢你们两位。还有，别乱扔垃圾。

turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 好。

turns.en: Joe, That was a really interesting conversation.
turns.zh: Joe，那真是一场很有意思的对话。

turns.en: Something that I don't think about that much, even though I'm in New York City all the time, how our trash actually gets collected. I do think there is an underlying political architecture that is like, there's a major political choice in having residential garbage not be pay as you go.
turns.zh: 这是我平时不太去想的事，尽管我一直待在纽约市——我们的垃圾究竟是怎么被收走的。我确实认为，其中有一种底层的政治架构，就是说，让住宅垃圾不采用“按量付费”，本身就是一个重大的政治选择。

turns.en: True, true.
turns.zh: 没错，没错。

turns.en: And so the big question is, do heavy wasters basically.
turns.zh: 所以那个大问题是，产生大量垃圾的人基本上……

turns.en: Get subsidized by people who aren't throwing.
turns.zh: ……是被那些不怎么扔垃圾的人……

turns.en: Out that much?
turns.zh: ……补贴了吗？

turns.en: No, you're right. There's a lot.
turns.zh: 不，你说得对。这里有很多……

turns.en: And, you know, we could have gotten into that question of, like, should it be completely, I guess, socialized.
turns.zh: 而且你知道的，我们本可以深入那个问题：就是，它是否应该被完全——我想——社会化（socialized）。

turns.en: One thing I appreciate, you know, people always whine.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏的一点是，你知道的，人们总是抱怨。

turns.en: They're like, oh, New York City paid a million and a half dollars to McKinsey to do a study on trash and they produced it.
turns.zh: 他们会说，哦，纽约市付了 150 万美元给 McKinsey 做一项关于垃圾的研究，然后就出了那个。

turns.en: Like, it's complicated.
turns.zh: 就是说，这事很复杂。

turns.en: And there's two things. One is collecting the data, et cetera. These are complicated things. And two, it would be kind of weird for a city to already have had that expertise in-house because you're not doing major studies of the trash system every year.
turns.zh: 而且有两点。一是收集数据等等，这些都是复杂的事。二是，一座城市本来就在内部养着那种专长，其实有点怪，因为你不会每年都做垃圾系统的大型研究。

turns.en: You hopefully.
turns.zh: 你顶多……

turns.en: maybe do this once every couple of decades or something like that.
turns.zh: ……每隔几十年做这么一次，或类似这样。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: So I don't know.
turns.zh: 所以我不知道。

turns.en: I'm very like, I think people have this knee jerk response. Like, why did, why did you pay another company and tell you that this is how they do it in Barcelona? Well, it's like, well, there's a lot of very interesting data. You know, this whole question of you asked the question, how do you switch from measuring weight of.
turns.zh: 我很，就是，我觉得人们有种本能的反应。就是，“为什么，为什么你们要付钱给另一家公司，让它告诉你们 Barcelona 是怎么做的？”嗯，这就像，嗯，这里面有很多非常有意思的数据。你知道的，你问的这整个问题——你怎么从测量垃圾的重量……

turns.en: Trash to volume of trash? How do you do that? It doesn't seem like a trivial question.
turns.zh: ……切换到测量垃圾的体积？你怎么做到？这看起来不是个小问题。

turns.en: I have no idea.
turns.zh: 我完全不知道。

turns.en: Bring in a bunch of, measurements, et cetera.
turns.zh: 要引入一堆测量等等。

turns.en: So I have an appreciation for like just the amount of sort of planning work that would have to go into this.
turns.zh: 所以我很能体会，光是这背后得投入多少规划工作。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: The other, the volumetric analysis seems really difficult to me. And despite that, they seem to have done it and, you know, they're getting a handle on what's needed. But the other thing that's really difficult or strikes me as very difficult is the placement of the bins.
turns.zh: 另外，那个体积分析在我看来真的很难。尽管如此，他们似乎做到了，而且你知道的，他们正在掌握所需的东西。但另一件真正难、或者说让我觉得非常难的事，是垃圾箱的布点。

turns.en: Yeah. Right.
turns.zh: 是啊。对。

turns.en: And this idea that you are actually changing New York's landscape, hopefully for the better. But in the meantime, you are taking up previously public space and having to figure out like the cost benefit analysis of doing that for literally every single building in.
turns.zh: 还有这个观念：你其实是在改变纽约的面貌，希望是往好的方向。但与此同时，你在占用原本的公共空间，还得为 literally 每一栋建筑算清楚这么做的成本收益分析。

turns.en: New York city.
turns.zh: 纽约市的每一栋建筑。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.en: That's pretty wild to think about just like how many blocks there are, but you know what? Like, I mean, I understand people park on the street and stuff like that, but that's socialized too. Why do, why do I, you know, that's really valuable real estate that some lucky people get to like park for.
turns.zh: 光是想想有多少个街区，就挺惊人的，但你知道吗？我是说，我理解人们在街上停车之类的，但那也是社会化的。为什么，为什么我——你知道的，那可是非常有价值的房地产，某些幸运的人却可以免费停在……

turns.en: Free, et cetera.
turns.zh: ……免费停车，等等。

turns.en: So, The only thing I'm going to miss is seeing the occasional rat eating.
turns.zh: 所以，我唯一会想念的，就是偶尔看到一只老鼠在啃……

turns.en: Pizza or something.
turns.zh: ……披萨什么的。

turns.en: You know, I'm really interested in the war on rats. You know, that was, I thought, something very, very inspiring during the Adams administration is seeing those numbers.
turns.zh: 你知道的，我对“灭鼠战”（war on rats）很感兴趣。你知道的，我觉得在 Adams 政府期间，非常非常鼓舞人心的一件事，就是看到那些……

turns.en: Of rat sightings.
turns.zh: ……老鼠目击的数字。

turns.zh: 我记得你在“灭鼠战”里是个单一议题选民（single issue voter）。

turns.en: Yeah, I was.
turns.zh: 是啊，我是。

turns.zh: 好吧。
